newsitem.title: BELGIUM: SOCCER-MAC THE KNIFE DRAGS BELGIAN TEAM OUT OF DOLDRUMS.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-MAC THE KNIFE DRAGS BELGIAN TEAM OUT OF DOLDRUMS.

text.p: For much of the past six years the Belgian soccer team has been ritually ridiculed, criticised and jeered.

Georges Leekens, who earned his nickname for his scything tackles in his glory days as Club Brugge and Belgium defender, was named national coach in January when Belgium were on the brink of elimination from the 1998 World Cup finals.

A brilliant communicator who was coaching first division newcomers Mouscron until his surprise nomination, Leekens moulded a solid new-look team who beat Wales 2-1 in Cardiff in March and Turkey 3-1 in Istanbul in late April.
"The ship is once again sailing on a good sea," Belgian soccer union president Michel D'Hooghe said.
"This team is ambitious again...it's to (Leekens's) merit to have injected group spirit and self confidence in a very short period of time."
Leekens, 48, commented: "I had to build on a quicksand of distrust. Some players were happy when others played badly, and worse, a deep fear was rooted in this team."

Leekens was like a breath of fresh air for Belgian media, relieved after years of mediocre matches which often ended in a chorus of disapproval and saw the team nosedive in FIFA's rankings from 18th place in mid-1993 to 44th early this year behind the likes of Japan and Zambia.
Former Anderlecht player Paul Van Himst, albeit reluctantly, took charge of a wavering Belgian side in 1991 after the retirement of veteran manager Guy Thys.

But Van Himst never managed to build a respectable line-up and although Belgium qualified for their fourth successive World Cup finals in 1994, he succumbed to a run of poor results and friction with key players.
Van Himst's assistant Wilfried Van Moer, also a former Belgian international, took over at the helm and won initial praise for his no-nonsense approach.

But he was soon criticised for his surly attitude towards media and players and was sacked in January after just nine months in charge -- a humiliating 3-0 home defeat by the Netherlands serving as the catalyst.
Leekens, who admitted he had been arrogant in the past but only to protect his clubs and players, by contrast proved a cunning entertainer and master in easing pressure on his players.

He played down a 3-0 defeat by Northern Ireland in a friendly in early March, saying it was too soon after his appointment to be significant, and skilfully weathered a burst of criticism over a seaside training camp which included carting and snooker sessions.

"Those people (who criticised) don't know anything about soccer," said Leekens, a former coach of Club Brugge and Anderlecht and Trabzonspor in Turkey. "As a coach you have to work on players' cohesion."
Leekens, who suffered a personal tragedy last August when his wife suffered a brain haemorrhage, warned against euphoria over the rejuvenated squad which now includes three Mouscron players.
"We still have a long way to go...In Cardiff and Istanbul we put two steps forward but we still don't have a world class team," said Leekens..
"Maybe we're not top class yet but everybody's giving what he's got. With such a mentality you can move mountains."
